newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CS says settlement discussed in Holocaust claims.
newsitem.headline: CS says settlement discussed in Holocaust claims.

text.p: Lawyers for both sides are discussing if a settlement is possible in a class action suit filed by representatives of Holocaust victims against Credit Suisse (CS) and two other big Swiss banks, CS officials said.
Credit Suisse chief executive Lukas Muehlemann said a settlement was a possibility but it depended on the conditions.
"I think we would favour an out of court settlement but it always depends on what the conditions would be," he told Reuters after presenting Credit Suisse Group's annual results.

"I think we would like to find a way of agreeing on a procedure which makes sense for both parties, but it will be a negotation which we will continue, and we will certainly not strive to (obtain) an out of court settlement at any price," Muehlemann added.
Asked whether there could be a resolution by any particular date, Muehlemann said: "There have been various dates set at various stages, and it would be unwise to comment."

Credit Suisse along with Union Bank of Switzerland and Swiss Bank Corp face three class-action suits filed in New York demanding several billion dollars The claimants allege that Swiss banks failed to pay back assets left by Holocaust victims.
A federal court judge has given the banks until May 15 to respond to the complaints.
Muehlemann said the Swiss banks were making good faith efforts to answer claims that they failed to pay out assets deposited for safe-keeping by Nazi victims.

"I think there is a total readiness from our side to put all the cards on the table," he said, adding Swiss banks had "committed to do that" with respect to two separate commissions looking into the matter of Holocaust claims.
The two commissions are a historical investigation headed by Swiss professor Jean-Francois Bergier and an independent bank probe headed by Paul Volcker, former chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve.
CS officials also said there could be some overlap between current investigations and the class action suit.
"We would hope to get some coordination between the class action suit and the investigation of the Volcker Commission," Muehlemann said.
CS chairman Rainer Gut, who has headed the drive by Swiss banks to set up a Swiss franc Holocaust fund, said Wednesday the banks are obliged to explain their role in World War II.
"A cover-up would be wrong," said Gut, adding banks would be guilty if they did not confront the issue in a public way.
CS officials also welcomed a government plan calling for revaluing Swiss gold reserves to provide basis for a humanitarian fund, announced on Wednesday.
"I am convinced this step will have a positive impact," said Gut, but said that there are still matters which much be dealt with for the banks. "It is not a quick fix," he said.
